title: M/S. Silver Collections P.Ltd vs M/S.The Aura Creations Exports P.Ltd on 19 January, 2026
full_text: M/S. Silver Collections P.Ltd vs M/S.The Aura Creations Exports P.Ltd on 19 January, 2026 IN THE COURT OF MS. BHAWNA RATTAN Judicial Magistrate First Class (NI Act) - 10 South West District; Dwarka Courts: New Delhi Date of Institution : 20.01.2018 Date of Reserving Judgment : 22.12.2025 Date of Judgment : 19.01.2026 In the matter of: M/S Silver Collections Private Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd 1. Regn. No. of Case : CC 3176/2018 2. CNR No. of Case : DLSW020037722018 3. Name of complainant : M/S Silver Collections Private Ltd. Through its directors Having office at: J-123 Bhaiyas 2nd Floor, Ashok Vihar, Phase I Delhi-110052 4. Name of accused : 1. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd. Through its directors: 2. Sh. Tarun Narang R/o D-11, Farm House, Satbari, Delhi-110030. 3. Smt. Ambika Narang R/o B-44, Greater Kailash Part I, New Delhi- 110048. Having its registered office at: D-11, Ansal Villas Satbari New Delhi-110030 5. Offence complained of : Under Section 138 NI Act Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: CC No.3176/2018 RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:04:40 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd +0530 page 1 of 16 6. Offence charged under : 138 NI Act Section 7 . Plea of accused person : Not guilty. 8. Final Order : ACQUITTED JUDGMENT Vide this judgment, I shall dispose of the complaint filed by the complainant under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. FACTS OF THE COMPLAINT 1. The complainant is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and authorised Sh. Rakesh Lahoti as authorised representative to appear in the present matter stated to be well acquainted and conversant with the facts of the case. 2. The accused/accused no.1 is a company and is run by its directors i.e. accused no. 2 and accused no. 3 had issued one cheque i.e. the cheque in question in favour of the complainant towards the discharge of the legal liability which accused owe to the complainant for the purchase of goods and also for the rent due. The accused also assured the complainant that the cheque will be honoured as and when presented for encashment. 3. However, when the complainant presented the cheque for encashment, it got dishonoured due to the reason "funds insufficient." The complainant then immediately informed the accused regarding the fate of the cheque and requested the accused to make the payment but the accused failed to Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: CC No.3176/2018 RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:04:45 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd +0530 page 2 of 16 pay any heed to the requests of the complainant. Thereafter the complainant sent a legal demand notice to the accused demanding the payment of the cheque amount but the accused failed to make any payment and thus the present complaint. PRE SUMMONING EVIDENCE 4. At the stage of pre-summoning evidence, the complainant relied upon the following documents: i. Board resolution Ex CW1/1. ii. Ledger statement Ex CW1/2 (colly). iii. Certificate under section 65 B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 Ex CW1/3. iv. Original cheque in question Ex CW1/4. v. Original return memo Ex CW1/5. vi. Copy of legal demand notice Ex CW1/6 (colly). vii. Original postal receipts Ex CW1/7 to Ex CW1/10. viii. Copy of AD card Ex CW1/11 to Ex CW1/12. ix. Tracking report Ex CW1/13 to Ex CW1/16. x. Master data sheet Ex CW1/17. After the PSE is led, the summoning of the accused is done if there is sufficient material on record in terms of the ingredients of the offence. i.e. once the complaint prima facie reveals that there is sufficient material on record to summon the accused, then the accused is summoned. The summoning order was done on 03.02.2018 and accused no. 3 i.e. Smt. Ambika Narang was not summoned. Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 CC No.3176/2018 15:04:50 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 3 of 16 APPEARANCE OF THE ACCUSED 5. For securing the appearance of the accused, summons issued. On the service of summons the accused no.2 (accused) entered into appearance, who also represented accused no.1 and the matter was referred to mediation for exploring the possibility of settlement. But matter could not be settled in mediation and hence proceeded on merits. Subsequently, the notice was framed. NOTICE FRAMING 6. Notice under section 251 of the code of criminal procedure ( CrPC ) was framed on 17.11.2021 and the same was read over and explained to accused and the accused was asked to make his plea of defence to which he stated; Our company rented the premises from the complainant. The cheque in question was handed over by one Mr. Vikram Khetan. I am not aware how this cheque came into the possession of the complainant. I was working as director of the accused company and Mr. Vikram Khetan is CFO. The complainant was also in possession of an advance amount of approximately Rs. 9 to 10 lakhs. I have no idea in what context the cheque in question was given to the complainant company. 7. The accused no. 2 admitted his signature on the cheque but denied the receipt of legal demand notice. Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:04:55 CC No.3176/2018 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 4 of 16 COMPLAINANT EVIDENCE (CE) 8. To prove the case of the complainant, the authorized representative (AR) who appeared on the behalf of the complainant was examined as CW1, and reiterated the version of the complaint and tendered his post-sum- moning evidence affidavit for the purpose of examination in chief as Ex CW1/B and relied upon all the documents furnished at the stage of pre- summoning evidence. STAGE OF CROSS EXAMINATION 9. For the purpose of cross examination, it is pertinent to mention the provision under section 145 (2) of the Negotiable Instruments, Act 1881; The court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the application of the prosecution or the accused, summon and examine any person giving evidence on affidavit as to the facts contained therein. 10. In the present matter, an oral prayer was made on behalf of accused under section 145 (2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for cross examination of the complainant and the court after considering the defence of the accused, allowed an opportunity to cross examine the complainant and the matter then fixed for cross examination of the complainant. 11.Thereafter the complainant i.e. CW1 was examined in chief on 29.10.2022 and partially cross examined. CW1 further cross examined on 28.06.2023 and was discharged. The complainant did not examine any other witness in CE. Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:04:59 +0530 CC No.3176/2018 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 5 of 16 RECORDING OF STATEMENT OF ACCUSED UNDER SECTION 313 of CrPC 12. At the stage of recording of statement of the accused under section 313 of CrPC all the incriminating circumstances/evidences are put to the accused so as to give him an opportunity to explain the same. The statement of the accused was recorded on 13.12.2023. 13.The accused at the time of recording of statement under section 313 of CrPC, stated as follows; Our company rented the premises from the complainant. The cheque in question was handed over by one Mr. Vikram Khetan. I am not aware how this cheque came into the possession of the complainant. I was working as director of the accused company and Mr. Vikram Khetan is CFO. The complainant was also in possession of an advance amount of approximately Rs. 9 to 10 lakhs. I have no idea in what context the cheque in question was given to the complainant company. .....I have not issued the cheque in question. One Mr. Vikram Khetan, CFO used to issue the cheques. DEFENCE EVIDENCE 14. At the time of recording of statement of the accused under section 313 of CrPC, the accused wished to lead the defence evidence (DE) and sought some time to move an application under section 315 of CrPC. 15.However, subsequently it was submitted on behalf of the accused that the accused do not want to examine any witness in DE. Thus, DE was closed. Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN RATTAN Date: CC No.3176/2018 2026.01.19 15:05:04 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 6 of 16 FINAL ARGUMENTS 16.In the final arguments, the complainant reiterated its entire case, that the accused handed over a cheque to the complainant in discharge of the liability i.e. the outstanding of the amount for the purchase of the goods by the accused and the rent was due. However, when the cheque in question was presented for encashment, the same was returned dishonoured. Thereafter the legal demand notice was also sent to the accused demanding the payment of the cheque amount. But the accused despite the receipt of the notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount. 17.While on the other hand, accused had refuted all the claims of the complainant on the ground that the accused owe no liability as alleged by the complainant. It was argued on the behalf of the accused that the complainant has not specifically clarified as regarding the liability of the accused. The complainant has not been able to prove its case and there are sufficient doubts in the case of the complainant. It was further argued that even the legal demand notice was defective as the complainant did not specify the goods which the accused bought from the complainant. 18.Written submissions filed only on behalf of the accused and the same is duly perused. APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE 19. Under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act 1881(hereinafter referred as Act), to held any person liable for the offence the following Digitally signed are the essential ingredients: by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 CC No.3176/2018 15:05:08 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 7 of 16 a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. 20. In the present matter, the cheque is dated 22.11.2017 and the same when presented for encashment was dishonoured vide return memo dated 23.11.2017 which means the same was presented within the statutory period of three months from the date on which it was drawn. Thereafter the complainant sent the legal demand notice dated 01.12.2017 to the accused for the demand of the payment and the same was sent on 21.12.2017 i.e. within statutory period of thirty days from the receipt of the information received regarding the dishonour of cheque. 21. The accused both at the time of framing of notice and recording of statement under section 313 of CrPC stated that, he did not receive the legal demand notice. However, the complainant has filed on record an AD card and the tracking report which reflected the service of legal demand notice to the accused. Further the proof of service furnished by the Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN RATTAN Date: 2026.01.19 CC No.3176/2018 15:05:12 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 8 of 16 complainant was not challenged by the accused. Also, in this regard it is relevant to mention the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, titled; 'C. C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed ' reported as (2007) 6 SCC 555; "13. According to Section 114 of the Act, read with Illustration (f) thereunder, when it appears to the Court that the common course of business renders it probable that a thing would happen, the Court may draw presumption that the thing would have happened, unless there are circumstances in a particular case to show that the common course of business was not followed. Thus, Section 114 enables the Court to presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in their relation to the facts of the particular case. Consequently, the court can presume that the common course of business has been followed in particular cases. When applied to communications sent by post, Section 114 enables the Court to presume that in the common course of natural events, the communication would have been delivered at the address of the addressee. But the presumption that is raised under Section 27 of the G.C. Act is a far stronger presumption. Further, while Section 114 of Evidence Act refers to a general presumption, Section 27 refers to a specific presumption. (Emphasis supplied.) "17 Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make the payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made the payment within 15 days of the receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complainant is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court alongwith the copy of complaint Under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section Digitally signed by BHAWNA CC No.3176/2018 BHAWNA RATTAN M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd RATTAN Date: 2026.01.19 15:05:17 +0530 page 9 of 16 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary Under Section 27 of General Clauses Act and 114 of the Evidence Act ." Hence, under the law there is presumption of the due service of the legal demand notice and the same has to be challenged and proved to the contrary by the accused. Thus, the third ingredient is also deemed to be established by the complainant. 22.Now, further in section 138 of the act, if the accused admits the fact that he has signed the cheque in question then the presumption under section 139 of the act, r/w section 118(a) of the act, arises. Section 139 Presumption in favour of holder; It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Section 118 Presumptions as to negotiable instruments; (a) of consideration - that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration. 23. In the present matter, the accused had admitted that the cheque bears his signature. However, the line of defence taken by the accused is that one Mr. Vikram Khetan who was the CFO (chief financial officer) used to issue the cheques and further the accused has no idea in what context, the cheque was given to the complainant. 24.Now, as per the mandate of the law, when the accused admits that he signed the cheque, then it is presumed that the same was given for a Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN CC No.3176/2018 RATTAN Date: 2026.01.19 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd 15:05:26 +0530 page 10 of 16 legally enforceable debt or other liability and presumption of the same lies in the favour of the complainant and to rebut the same presumption the burden of proof lies on the accused. 25.The burden of presumption can be discharged by the accused by preponderance of probabilities either through the cross examination of the complainant or by leading his own evidence at the stage of defence evidence. 26.Now in the present matter since the right to cross examine the complainant was given to the accused, thus the AR of the complainant examined as CW1. During the examination in chief, CW1 adopted the post summoning evidence affidavit i.e. Ex CW1/B and reiterated the same facts as mentioned in the complaint qua the liability of the accused. Majorly the case of the complainant is that the accused issued the cheque in question in discharge of the legal liability which the accused owe towards the purchase of goods i.e. yarn from the complainant and also the rent was due to the complainant since the premises of the complainant was taken on rent by the accused. The fact of rented premises is also admitted by the accused. 27.During the cross examination, CW1 stated that the present case pertains to the outstanding of purchase of yarn goods and the rent. Now, will reproduce some relevant portion of the cross examination of CW1; "..............., the accused company used to raise requests of purchase order sometimes through E-mail and also through telephone to the complainant company. I have not filed any purchase order on record. When the purchase order is raised by the accused company, the complainant company used to generate a bill and Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 CC No.3176/2018 15:05:31 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 11 of 16 thereafter the goods were supplied to the complainant company through their transport. .............. I have not filed any invoice generated by the complainant pertaining to the transaction to the present case. Volt. We have filed the ledger A/c Ex CW1/2 reflecting the transactions of the accused company. (At this stage the witness is going through the Ex CW1/2 in judicial file.) Ex CW1/2 does not mention any entry with respect to supply of yarn by the complainant company." At this stage, will pause and appreciate the testimony of CW1 qua the liability of the outstanding amount of the purchase of the goods i.e. yarn. The complainant had not placed on record any invoice or purchase order to show that any/some goods as claimed by the complainant were purchased by the accused and there was an outstanding due for that purchased goods. 28.Further CW1 testified that the ledger account of the accused is placed on record as Ex CW1/2 and when the witness was confronted with the same, no such entry was highlighted by the witness with respect to the supply of yarn or purchase of yarn by the accused qua which liability the complainant has filed the present case. 29.Indisputably, the holder of a negotiable instrument is deemed to be holder in due course but the liability must be 'legal' liability. In " Rajesh Jain vs Ajay Singh " reported as (2023) 10 SCC 148; it has been held by the court; 45. Therefore, in fine, it can be said that once the accused adduces evidence to the satisfaction of the Court that on a preponderance of probabilities there exists no debt/liability in the manner Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: CC No.3176/2018 RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:05:36 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd +0530 page 12 of 16 pleaded in the complaint or the demand notice or the affidavit-evidence, the burden shifts to the complainant and the presumption 'disappears' and does not haunt the accused any longer. The onus having now shifted to the complainant, he will be obliged to prove the existence of a debt/liability as a matter of fact and his failure to prove would result in dismissal of his complaint case. Thereafter, the presumption under section 139 does not again come to the complainant's rescue. Once both parties have adduced evidence, the Court has to consider the same and the burden of proof loses all its importance. (Emphasis Supplied) The Hon'ble Court had abundantly made it clear that debt/liability must be the one as pleaded in the complaint and if the liability did not exist in the manner as claimed then certainly the burden shifts to the complainant to prove his case. 30.Now will continue with the further cross examination of CW1 and reproduce the relevant portion; "I have not filed any lease/rent entered by the complainant with the accused. The accused had vacated the rented premises in 2017-2018. I cannot admit or deny that the complainant company has received one month advance rent and three months security amount......." Now, qua the outstanding of rent, no rent or lease agreement has been filed by the complainant to show and to bring on record the exact amount or for the period, the rent was due to the complainant. Although the ledger shows some entries related to rent. However, in the absence of any corroborative evidence it is difficult to place sole reliance on the ledger for the purpose of adjudication. Also, the other aspect which remained unclear that the witness/CW1 neither admitted nor denied that the complainant had received three months of rent as security amount, which again gives benefit of reasonable doubt to the accused. Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN CC No.3176/2018 Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd 15:05:41 +0530 page 13 of 16 Indeed, the factum of security amount can be taken note of, as it is a general practice at the time of giving the premises on rent. 31.Further, with regard to the evidentiary aspect of the ledger account, abundant caution has to be taken. There are plenty of judgments pronounced by the Constitutional Courts through which the position has been made clear as, it has been reiterated by the Courts that, ledger account in itself is not a cogent proof unless it is corroborated by clinching evidence. There must be some supporting document to impute the liability. Also, in general parlance, ledger is a self-made document by the party itself and thus, cannot be used as self-serving admission. Hence, qua the outstanding of purchase amount of the goods/yarn, I have no hesitation in concluding, that by cross examination the accused has raised a reasonable doubt in the case of the complainant. 32. Interestedly, in the cross examination CW1 also stated, "I cannot say at present the exact amount which was outstanding at the time of filing of the present case with respect to yarn and the rent. Volt. The amount which is being claimed in the cheque in question has been arrived with respect to the outstanding of yarn and rent along with interest." Now this statement of CW1 seems that the complainant is trying to shoot an arrow in the dark. It could have been better, if the complainant had properly bifurcated the liability. 33.The law is amply clear. The liability has to be exact liability. A person simply cannot be imputed with any random liability. In "Kaveri Plastics vs Mahdoom Bawa Bahurudeen Noorul" reported as 2025 INSC 1133, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed; Digitally signed by BHAWNA RATTAN BHAWNA Date: RATTAN 2026.01.19 15:05:44 +0530 CC No.3176/2018 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 14 of 16 6.4 The proposition that the penal provision has to be construed strictly was again asserted by this Court in K.K. Ahuja vs. V.K. Vora & Anr. (2009)10 SCC 48. In the context of provision of Sections 141 and 138 of the NI Act it was observed in para 17 of the judgment that penal statutes are to be construed strictly and that if conditions are scraped, the courts will insist upon strict literal compliance. It was stated that there is no question of inferential or implied compliance. (emphasis supplied) Hence, the penal provisions are always to be strictly complied with and the liability must be strictly proved. 34.Hence, after appreciating the facts of the complaint and the testimony of the witness/CW1, there is no difficulty in saying that there are shortcomings/inconsistencies in the case of the complainant which undeniably has shifted the burden back to the complainant to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. 35.The accused has not led the defence evidence. Needless to mention that by cross examination of the complainant, the accused already discharged its burden of presumption by preponderance of probabilities. 36.Now, since the onus has shifted back to the complainant to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, thus the complainant case must now stand on its own legs. The complainant/CW1 however has failed to furnish any further cogent evidence either orally or in writing to show and prove the liability as claimed. 37.Thus, in the absence of any credible witness or evidence it is difficult to impute criminal liability on the accused and it can be said that the complainant has failed to prove its case in the light of the settled principle Digitally signed by BHAWNA BHAWNA RATTAN RATTAN Date: 2026.01.19 CC No.3176/2018 15:05:49 +0530 M/S Silver Collections Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/S The Aura Creations Export Pvt. Ltd page 15 of 16 of criminal law that the accused is innocent until proven guilty, beyond reasonable doubt. 38.Therefore, in the light of the principles of law, the totality of facts, I am of the view, that accused is not guilty of the offence under section 138 of the Act, and thus accused M/s The Aura Creations Exports Pvt. Ltd. through its director Tarun Narang is hereby acquitted.
